text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Russian newspapers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
KOMMERSANT DAILY
- The government makes public a list of the seven most urgent issues on its working agenda and says it will not print money to bridge budget gaps.
- A new decree on land ownership, supposed to push forward the stagnating real estate market, is so poorly worded that it could do the opposite unless it is spelled out properly.
- First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov is bringing more and more people from his native stronghold of Nizhny Novgorod to Moscow.
- IMF directors in Washington approve a programme of economic development for Russia submitted by Moscow.
- A World Bank delegation has been given a chance to get first-hand information on the way its credits to Moscow have been used.
- Commercial banks in charge of distributing budget payments have asked Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov to lobby against a decree introducing a fee for handling state money.
- A new car assembly plant in Kaliningrad on the Baltic sea inaugurated by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has yet to prove that it is a viable operation.
- A non-state pension fund may become a key element in a new reformed pension system in Russia.
SEVODNYA
- The government is setting daunting tasks for itself and announcing them in public, a move which may put the prime minister and his first deputies in the line of fire.

- The government, desperate to get the second tranche of a credit-line to boost reform in the coal industry, has had to show World Bank inspectors the grim picture of Russian coalminers' everyday life.
- Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov says the city will be extremely cautious in implementing new land ownership regulations.
- Russian meat importers, yielding to the scare of mad cow disease, are moving away from European beef producers.
- Tax authorities have no real means to force companies with big tax backlogs to contribute to the budget and keep their fingers crossed that the new tax code will remedy the situation.
- Western banks grant a $1 billion credit to Gazprom in a spectacular display of confidence that the natural gas monopoly remains a viable company despite friction with authorities in Moscow.
- The cheapest Korean-brand car to be assembled at a newly-opened plant in Kaliningrad on the Baltic will cost $9,000.
NEZAVISIMAYA GAZETA
- The economy ministry will control tenders on deliveries for state needs.
- Heavy machine-building is crawling out of crisis.
- The government has accepted the idea of slightly higher inflation in 1997.
- Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev says he will put an end to a situation where problems plaguing Russia's Far East are de facto considered to be of secondary importance.
ROSSIISKAYA GAZETA
- The area under crop in Russia this year will not be less than in 1996.
MOSKOVSKY KOMSOMOLETS
- A poultry sickness is sweeping through poultry farms around Moscow.
- Opposition Duma deputies say budget cuts proposed by the government cannot be accepted unless ways to increase revenues are worked out.
--Andrei Shukshin, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
